The biggest misread of anyone predicting the end of software engineering was imagining that the world only needed a certain amount of software, and bringing automation to the field would reduce the need for labor. 

Exactly the opposite is happening where essentially most things are actually turning into software. Because agents can use tools, work with computers, write software on the fly, and process data like humans (but far faster), we can now throw “software” at problems that never could reasonably be digitized before.

What that leads to is the role of engineering taking on greater importance in the economy, because we can now engineer far more systems and processes than were possible before.

If you’re a bank trying to do new forms of trading, engineers are often your first bet. If you are in life sciences, you expect more and more research and lab work to be engineering centric. If you’re in manufacturing, you’re trying to automate more of the supply chain, all that is engineering. More and more work is shaped like software problems.

Yes we’re not going to be coding manually in the future. But almost everything will be code, which means those that understand it are in a fantastic position.

It’s incredible to have reached a threshold where it’s practical that AI will be better at training models than humans are so quickly. One day recursive self improvement feels far off, and the next we already have signs of what it will look like.

Model capability finally exceeding most human engineers, advancements in the harness and infra for long running agents, a growing array of data, and the ability to parallelize the agents to work on vastly more tasks and tests and approaches than any person could have before, creates an incredible flywheel. 

This flywheel will almost certainly accelerate model progress far faster than we’ve seen before - or at a minimum enable pushing up the ceiling of the frontier at an insane rate. If you aren’t pricing in what RSI will lead to, that’s probably a mistake.

- Reflection debuts with Beam 1.0, the #1 US open model on Agent Arena overall.

Arena Alignment Index rankings by lab:

- #7 @reflection_ai: Beam-1.0-501B-A23B at 75.3%

Exciting news: Muse Spark Open (Max) by @AIatMeta is the #1 US open model in the Code Arena: WebDev! With 1511 pts, it’s #13 among open models overall.

Priced at $1.25/$4.25 per 1M input/output tokens, it’s 79% less than Muse Wonder (Max) and priced on par with Muse Spark 1.3 (Max).

By domain, Muse Spark Open (Max) ranks:
- #13 in Brand & Marketing, and in Data & Analytics
- #14 in Reference-Based Design
- #15 Gaming, and in Consumer Product
- #20 in Simulations

Congrats to the team at @AIatMeta on this contribution to the open ecosystem!

There are people who say “the changes from AI will take longer than you think because <bottlenecks and institutions and other broad abstractions>,” who also were inclined to believe that AI cyber was an exaggerated risk after GLM 5.3’s weights were public for ~days. This seems like motivated reasoning; you cannot say, “ah, you shouldn’t worry about AI risks overwhelming us through speed alone, because <bottlenecks and diffusion>,” and then also make pronouncements about AI risks after a few days of evidence.

a lot of the shortcomings we are seeing with coding agents today ultimately boil down to limitations in post training

why agents don’t write good tests by default? why do they spit out a ton of useless comments? why do vibe coded codebases all turn into a mess without human steering and intervention? 

because in current RLVR pipelines, we reward task resolution. as long as the agents wrote code that could pass predefined hidden tests, that’s a success

whether the architecture is clean, whether the code is easy to maintain and evolve, whether the comments are actually helpful in future work, whether the test cases help catch real problems down the road - none of these make a difference in how the model was rewarded when the reward is done at task level

we have been “fixing” a lot of these problems with system prompts, skills, and harness features, which is very necessary in the near term

but i think eventually the post training pipeline will keep evolving and take more and more of these long term considerations into account

when it does, we will finally have agents that can write good code by default. anyone will be able to build very complex software as long as they can articulate their intent clearly

experienced engineers will not have an advantage any more just because they know a little more than average people on how to write good code (including myself)

and i think that’ll be a very beautiful world
